blocks.text:
Design a short-video platform like TikTok, centered on a For You feed that shows an endless stream of short videos a viewer swipes through, one after another. Unlike the news feed problem earlier in this project, which showed posts from accounts a user explicitly follows, this feed's defining trait is that most of what a viewer sees comes from creators they have never followed at all, driven instead by a recommendation system inferring their interests from behavior, primarily how long they actually watch, rather than from a social graph.

The technique that makes this both relevant and fast at massive scale is a two-stage retrieve-then-rank recommendation pipeline, a lightweight candidate generation stage narrows hundreds of millions of videos down to a few hundred plausible ones, and only then does a heavier ranking model spend real computation scoring that much smaller set.

Unlike the news feed problem earlier in this project, which showed posts from accounts a user explicitly follows, this feed's defining trait is that most of what a viewer sees comes from creators they have never followed at all, driven instead by a recommendation system inferring their interests from behavior, primarily how long they actually watch, rather than from a social graph.

The technique that makes this both relevant and fast at massive scale is a two-stage retrieve-then-rank recommendation pipeline, a lightweight candidate generation stage narrows hundreds of millions of videos down to a few hundred plausible ones, and only then does a heavier ranking model spend real computation scoring that much smaller set.

blocks.text: A user should be able to upload a short video, which is processed and becomes eligible for recommendation once it clears content moderation. A viewer should be able to open a For You feed and continuously swipe through an endless stream of recommended videos. The system should learn from implicit signals, primarily watch time and completion, rather than requiring explicit likes to understand what a viewer is interested in. A video already shown to a viewer in their current session should not be shown to them again in that same session.

blocks.text: Five qualities matter here, and the first is what most separates this design from every prior feed-style problem in this project.
blocks.content: Five qualities matter here, and the first is what most separates this design from every prior feed-style problem in this project.

blocks.alt: Discovery over the social graph, responsiveness to recent behavior, seamless and instant swiping, scalable recommendation at massive corpus size, and content safety before recommendation

blocks.text: Discovery over the social graph means most of what a viewer sees genuinely has nothing to do with who they follow, unlike a social news feed. Responsiveness to recent behavior means what a viewer just watched should meaningfully influence what they see next, even within the same session, not only in some future visit. Seamless, instant swiping means moving to the next video must never feel like a visible loading pause, the client experience depends on it. Scalable recommendation at massive corpus size means scoring every single one of hundreds of millions of eligible videos for every individual feed request is simply not computationally feasible. And content safety before recommendation means a video must clear moderation before it is ever eligible to be shown to anyone at all.

Scalable recommendation at massive corpus size means scoring every single one of hundreds of millions of eligible videos for every individual feed request is simply not computationally feasible. And content safety before recommendation means a video must clear moderation before it is ever eligible to be shown to anyone at all.

blocks.text: This design assumes video transcoding, storage, and CDN delivery are handled by the same underlying pipeline this project's other video-streaming designs already cover, and focuses instead on what is genuinely new here, discovery-driven recommendation. Recommendation is assumed to be a two-stage retrieve-then-rank pipeline, a fast candidate generation stage followed by a heavier ranking stage, rather than scoring the full corpus directly. Session-level de-duplication is assumed to be strict, a video already shown in the current session is excluded from candidate generation for the remainder of that session.

Session-level de-duplication is assumed to be strict, a video already shown in the current session is excluded from candidate generation for the remainder of that session.

blocks.text: A platform at real scale might have hundreds of millions of eligible videos in its corpus at any given time, growing continuously as new uploads clear moderation. A single viewing session generates a continuous stream of feed requests as a user swipes through many videos in quick succession, each request needing to feel instantaneous. Candidate generation narrows that enormous corpus down to a few hundred plausible candidates before any heavier ranking computation runs at all, and watch events, generated on essentially every single video viewed, vastly outnumber explicit signals like likes or comments as the dominant source of interest information.

blocks.alt: Hundreds of millions of eligible videos in the corpus, continuous rapid-fire feed requests per session, candidate generation narrowing to a few hundred before heavy ranking, and watch events dominating as the primary interest signal

blocks.text: An uploaded video passes through content moderation before entering the transcoding pipeline and video storage, only becoming eligible for recommendation once cleared. A viewer's feed request goes through candidate generation, narrowing the eligible corpus down using lightweight signals, and a ranking model then scores that smaller candidate set by predicted watch time to produce the final ordered feed. Every watch event flows back through an implicit signal collector that updates the viewer's own interest profile, directly shaping future candidate generation.

blocks.alt: An uploaded video clears moderation before becoming recommendation-eligible; a feed request runs through candidate generation and ranking to produce an ordered feed, while watch events continuously update the viewer's interest profile

blocks.text: Rather than scoring every eligible video in the corpus for every single feed request, candidate generation uses lightweight signals, a viewer's own interest tags and the watch history of similar viewers, to narrow hundreds of millions of videos down to a few hundred plausible candidates.

blocks.text: Only the much smaller candidate set produced by candidate generation is passed to a heavier ranking model, which predicts each candidate's likely watch time and completion probability for this specific viewer, producing the final ordered feed for this specific request.

blocks.text: While a viewer is still watching the current video, the client silently prefetches the next several videos in the already-ranked feed, so that whenever the viewer actually swipes, the next video is already locally ready to play instantly.

blocks.text: The feed endpoint deliberately returns a batch of already fully-ranked videos rather than a single one at a time, which is exactly what makes client-side prefetching of the next several videos possible without an extra round trip per swipe.

blocks.alt: Video, tracking whether it has cleared moderation, WatchEvent recording how much of a video a user actually watched, and InterestProfile summarizing a user's current top interest tags

blocks.text: InterestProfile is deliberately a small, continuously-updated summary rather than the full raw watch history, since candidate generation needs to read it on essentially every feed request and cannot afford to reprocess a viewer's entire history each time.
blocks.content: InterestProfile is deliberately a small, continuously-updated summary rather than the full raw watch history, since candidate generation needs to read it on essentially every feed request and cannot afford to reprocess a viewer's entire history each time.

blocks.text: Watch events are recorded at a fine enough granularity, watch fraction rather than only a binary watched-or-not flag, to distinguish a video someone watched for one second from one they watched to completion and replayed, a meaningfully different and far stronger interest signal. Video moderation status is modeled as a hard, boolean gate rather than a soft ranking penalty, since an unmoderated video must never be recommendable at all, regardless of any other signal about it.

blocks.text: The happy path is the For You feed flow above, candidate generation narrows the corpus, ranking orders the result, and the client prefetches ahead for seamless swiping. The workflow worth walking through separately is how quickly behavior actually changes recommendations, a single strong signal, watching one video all the way through and rewatching it, updates the viewer's interest profile promptly enough that the very next batch of candidates already reflects it, which is exactly what makes this feed feel responsive within a single session rather than only improving slowly over days.

blocks.alt: A video segment already cached at a nearby CDN edge is served instantly; one that is not yet cached is fetched from origin storage once and cached at the edge for subsequent viewers

blocks.text: This is the same CDN edge-caching pattern this project's other video-streaming designs already use, popular videos are watched by an enormous number of viewers, making edge caching a very high-value optimization here as well.

blocks.alt: A watch or completion event is placed on a signal ingestion queue, consumed by workers that update the viewer's interest profile, which candidate generation then reads from

blocks.text: Queuing signal processing, rather than updating an interest profile synchronously within the watch-event request itself, keeps reporting a watch event fast regardless of how much downstream signal processing that event ultimately triggers.
blocks.content: Queuing signal processing, rather than updating an interest profile synchronously within the watch-event request itself, keeps reporting a watch event fast regardless of how much downstream signal processing that event ultimately triggers.

blocks.alt: A feed request is routed by hashing the viewer's user id, so a given viewer's recent session context is consistently handled by the same recommendation instance

blocks.text: Routing consistently by viewer, rather than plain round-robin, lets a recommendation instance keep a viewer's current session's already-shown-video set close at hand without needing a separate lookup on every single request.
blocks.content: Routing consistently by viewer, rather than plain round-robin, lets a recommendation instance keep a viewer's current session's already-shown-video set close at hand without needing a separate lookup on every single request.

blocks.alt: Rising candidate generation or ranking latency triggers adding more instances of whichever stage is falling behind

blocks.text: Because candidate generation and ranking are two separate stages with very different computational costs, each can be scaled independently, adding more candidate-generation capacity as the corpus grows, and more ranking capacity as feed request volume grows, without over-provisioning either for the other's needs.

blocks.text: Interest profiles are small, frequently read, and frequently updated, scaling as a user-partitioned, low-latency store. The video corpus and its moderation status scale as a much larger, read-heavy store that candidate generation continuously queries, growing steadily as new uploads clear moderation.
blocks.content: Interest profiles are small, frequently read, and frequently updated, scaling as a user-partitioned, low-latency store. The video corpus and its moderation status scale as a much larger, read-heavy store that candidate generation continuously queries, growing steadily as new uploads clear moderation.

blocks.alt: What the recommendation model currently believes about a viewer's interests is eventually consistent, updated shortly after a watch event; whether a video is actually eligible to be recommended at all is strongly required, never a soft or approximate gate

blocks.text: This mirrors this project's recurring pattern of splitting a soft, best-effort signal, here a rapidly evolving interest profile, from a hard, non-negotiable gate, here content moderation clearance, that must never be bypassed no matter how strong any other signal about a video looks.

blocks.alt: If candidate generation is temporarily degraded, the feed falls back to a simpler, cached candidate set, such as currently trending videos, rather than showing an empty or broken feed

blocks.text: This fallback is what keeps a viewer's experience gracefully degraded rather than broken when the more sophisticated recommendation path is unavailable, a reasonable, if less personalized, feed is always better than none at all.
blocks.content: This fallback is what keeps a viewer's experience gracefully degraded rather than broken when the more sophisticated recommendation path is unavailable, a reasonable, if less personalized, feed is always better than none at all.

blocks.alt: A newly uploaded video that fails content moderation is never recommendable or publicly viewable at all; one that clears moderation enters the pool candidate generation can actually draw from

blocks.text: Content moderation as a hard gate before recommendation eligibility is this design's defining security concern, distinct from every other category's angle in this project, since a recommendation system that can surface harmful content to a massive audience before anyone reviews it is a fundamentally different kind of risk than a technical vulnerability.

blocks.text: Candidate generation and ranking latency, tracked separately, are the clearest signals of whether the two-stage pipeline is keeping the feed feeling instant. Aggregate watch-completion rate across the platform is worth watching as a broad recommendation-quality signal, a meaningful drop often means something in the pipeline has genuinely regressed, not just ordinary day-to-day variance.

blocks.alt: Candidate generation having to search an enormous, constantly growing video corpus, ranking model latency directly delaying every feed request, and a content moderation backlog delaying new videos' eligibility

blocks.text: The first of these is directly mitigated by candidate generation's own design, using lightweight, precomputed signals specifically so that narrowing the corpus never means a full, live scan of every eligible video for every single request.

blocks.text: The two-stage pipeline is the right default because it is the only approach that keeps both genuine recommendation quality and real-time feed latency achievable at once, at real corpus scale, a single-stage design is forced to sacrifice one or the other.
blocks.content: The two-stage pipeline is the right default because it is the only approach that keeps both genuine recommendation quality and real-time feed latency achievable at once, at real corpus scale, a single-stage design is forced to sacrifice one or the other.

blocks.text: Candidate generation itself is the largest cost optimization in this design, converting an otherwise infeasible full-corpus scoring problem into a small, affordable ranking problem. CDN edge caching for popular videos, shared with this project's other video-streaming designs, avoids repeatedly serving the same, most-watched content from origin storage.

blocks.text: A change to the ranking model needs careful, gradual rollout with real before-and-after watch-time measurement, since a regression here directly affects what every viewer sees on every single swipe. Changes to content moderation rules need particularly careful, monitored rollout too, since either an overly permissive or an overly restrictive change has real, immediate consequences for what becomes recommendation-eligible platform-wide.

blocks.text: Richer candidate generation signals, incorporating video content embeddings for genuine content-based similarity rather than only tag matching and collaborative signals, would likely surface more relevant candidates than today's simpler approach. Cross-session interest decay, gradually reducing the weight of an old interest signal that a viewer has clearly moved on from, would keep long-term recommendations feeling current rather than anchored to stale behavior.

items: Architecture: a two-stage recommendation pipeline, lightweight candidate generation followed by heavier ranking, feeding an ordered For You feed with client-side prefetching for seamless swiping.
Capacity: hundreds of millions of eligible videos, continuous rapid-fire feed requests per session, and watch events dominating as the primary interest signal.
The core techniques: two-stage retrieve-then-rank recommendation and session-level de-duplication, both worked through with a real, verified implementation in Java, Python, and C++.
Database: a small, frequently-updated per-user interest profile alongside a much larger, read-heavy video corpus gated by moderation status.
End-to-end workflows: a normal For You feed request and an implicit signal update flow, both traced as sequence diagrams.
Consistency: an eventually consistent, rapidly evolving interest profile paired with a strongly enforced, non-negotiable content moderation gate.
Trade-offs: two-stage retrieve-then-rank versus scoring the entire corpus directly versus a traditional follow-graph feed, compared directly on latency and recommendation quality.
